Git stopped because the two sets of commits you're trying to combine share no common ancestor. Git merges work by finding a shared past commit and combining the changes made since then. When there's no shared commit, it has no basis for a merge and refuses by default, since this usually means something is wrong.

Common causes:

- You ran `git init` in a folder to start a project, then added a remote that already had its own history, and pulled or merged it.
- You're trying to merge two repositories that were created separately.
- The remote was recreated or re-initialized, so its history no longer connects to your local copy.

To check, you can run:

```
git log --oneline --all
git remote -v
```

If the commit histories look like two separate projects and you do want to combine them, you can override the check:

```
git pull --allow-unrelated-histories
# or
git merge --allow-unrelated-histories <branch>
```

Before you do, make sure you're pulling from the right remote. Merging unrelated histories often produces conflicts on files that exist in both, such as a README or `.gitignore`, so review the result carefully.
